chapter_title: Introduction to Lua Syntax and Variables
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the exciting world of Lua scripting in Roblox! This chapter marks your first step into bringing your Roblox creations to life with code. Lua is the scripting language Roblox uses, and it's chosen for its simplicity, speed, and efficiency, making it an excellent language for game development. Don't worry if you're new to programming; Lua is designed to be easy to learn, and we'll build your understanding step by step. Our journey begins with the very basics: understanding how Lua code is structured and how we store information using variables.

At its core, Lua syntax is quite straightforward. Unlike some other languages, semicolons at the end of statements are generally optional in Lua, though you might see them used by some developers for clarity or habit. The most crucial aspect of Lua syntax is its case sensitivity. `myVariable` is entirely different from `myvariable`, so pay close attention to capitalization! Comments are also vital for making your code understandable to yourself and others. In Lua, single-line comments begin with two hyphens (`--`), and multi-line comments are enclosed between `--[[` and `--]]`. For instance, `-- This is a single-line comment` or `print("Hello") -- This prints a message`. For multi-line comments, you might write: `--[[ This is a longer explanation that spans multiple lines. It's great for documenting complex functions. --]]`. Good commenting practices are a cornerstone of clean, maintainable code, especially as your Roblox games grow in complexity.

Variables are essentially named containers for storing data. Think of them like labeled boxes where you can put different types of information, such as a player's score, the name of an item, or whether a door is open or closed. In Lua, you declare a variable by simply assigning a value to a name. For example, `playerScore = 0` creates a variable named `playerScore` and assigns it the initial value of `0`. A critical concept in Lua is variable scope. By default, if you don't specify `local`, a variable is considered global. Global variables can be accessed and modified from anywhere in your script, or even from other scripts in your game, which can sometimes lead to unintended side effects or conflicts. To prevent this, it's best practice to declare variables as `local` whenever possible. A `local` variable exists only within the block of code where it's defined (e.g., inside a function or a specific `do...end` block), making your code more organized and less prone to errors. For instance, `local playerName = "RobloxDev"` creates a local variable `playerName`.

Lua supports several fundamental data types to handle different kinds of information. The `number` type handles all numerical values, whether they are integers (whole numbers like `10`, `100`) or floating-point numbers (decimals like `3.14`, `0.5`). The `string` type is used for text, which must always be enclosed in single (`'`) or double (`"`) quotes. For example, `local gameTitle = "My Awesome Obby"`. The `boolean` type represents truth values: `true` or `false`. These are incredibly useful for conditional logic, such as checking if a player has enough coins (`hasEnoughCoins = true`). Finally, `nil` is a special type that represents the absence of a value. If a variable hasn't been assigned a value, it defaults to `nil`. You can also explicitly set a variable to `nil` to effectively "delete" its value and free up memory. Understanding these types is crucial because operations you perform on variables often depend on their type. Trying to add a number to a string, for example, will typically result in an error unless explicitly converted.

With variables in hand, you can start performing operations. Basic arithmetic operations in Lua are straightforward: addition (`+`), subtraction (`-`), multiplication (`*`), division (`/`), modulo (remainder, `%`), and exponentiation (`^`). For example, `local totalScore = playerScore + 100` or `local remainingHealth = maxHealth - damageTaken`. String manipulation is also very common in game development. In Lua, you concatenate (join) strings using the double-dot operator (`..`). So, `local greeting = "Hello, " .. playerName .. "!"` would combine the literal strings with the value of `playerName`. It's important to remember that you can only concatenate strings with other strings. If you try to concatenate a number directly, Lua will attempt to convert it to a string first, but it's often safer and clearer to explicitly convert numbers to strings using `tostring()` if you're unsure, e.g., `local message = "Your score is: " .. tostring(playerScore)`.

A common mistake beginners make is forgetting the `local` keyword, especially when working in Roblox Studio. If you define a variable without `local` inside a function or a loop, it becomes global, potentially overwriting another variable with the same name elsewhere in your game, leading to hard-to-debug issues. Always default to `local` unless you specifically need a global variable. Another frequent error is type mismatch. For instance, trying to perform arithmetic on a string that isn't a valid number will cause a runtime error. Always ensure your data types are compatible with the operations you're attempting. Roblox Studio's output window is your best friend here; it will often provide helpful error messages that point you to the line of code causing the problem. Learning to read and understand these error messages is a vital skill for any developer.

```lua
-- Chapter 2.1: Introduction to Lua Syntax and Variables

-- Single-line comment example
-- This script demonstrates basic Lua syntax and variable usage in Roblox.

--[[
    This is a multi-line comment.
    It's useful for providing more detailed explanations
    about a section of code or a script's purpose.
]]

-- 1. Declaring and initializing local variables (best practice!)
local gameTitle = "My First Roblox Game" -- string data type
local playerScore = 0                   -- number data type (integer)
local isGameActive = true               -- boolean data type
local lastPlayerJoined = nil            -- nil data type (no value yet)

-- 2. Demonstrating variable assignment and modification
print("Initial Player Score: " .. playerScore)
playerScore = playerScore + 50 -- Update score
print("New Player Score: " .. playerScore)

-- 3. Working with different data types
local playerHealth = 100.0 -- number data type (float)
local playerName = "Robloxian123" -- string data type

-- 4. Basic arithmetic operations
local enemyDamage = 25
playerHealth = playerHealth - enemyDamage
print(playerName .. "'s Health after damage: " .. playerHealth)

local totalCoins = 150
local coinsPerLevel = 10
local levelsCompleted = totalCoins / coinsPerLevel -- Division
print("Levels completed: " .. levelsCompleted)

local remainderCoins = totalCoins % coinsPerLevel -- Modulo (remainder)
print("Remaining coins after full levels: " .. remainderCoins)

-- 5. String concatenation
local welcomeMessage = "Welcome, " .. playerName .. " to " .. gameTitle .. "!"
print(welcomeMessage)

-- Example of a common mistake: forgetting 'local' (avoid this in real code!)
-- badGlobalVariable = "I can be accessed anywhere and might cause conflicts!"
-- print(badGlobalVariable)

-- Example of type conversion for concatenation (good practice)
local currentLevel = 5
local levelUpMessage = "Congratulations, " .. playerName .. "! You reached Level " .. tostring(currentLevel) .. "!"
print(levelUpMessage)

-- Checking variable type
print("Type of playerScore: " .. type(playerScore))
print("Type of gameTitle: " .. type(gameTitle))
print("Type of isGameActive: " .. type(isGameActive))
print("Type of lastPlayerJoined: " .. type(lastPlayerJoined))
```

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson we take your first steps into Lua, the scripting language used in Roblox. You'll learn how Lua code is written, how to add comments, and how to create variables that store numbers, text, booleans, or no value at all. We'll show why the local keyword matters and how simple operations like addition or string joining let you update player state. A concrete example you'll see repeatedly is tracking a player's score: we start with a number variable set to zero and update it when the player collects coins. We'll also cover common beginner mistakes, such as forgetting local which can create surprising global conflicts, and type mismatches that cause runtime errors when you try to do math with text. By the end of this chapter you'll understand basic Lua syntax rules, the main data types, how to do arithmetic and string concatenation, and why scope keeps your scripts predictable. Think of this as the toolbox you need to make small scripts that behave reliably as your game grows.

keyIdea.title: Start small, stay local
keyIdea.text: Use clear variable names and prefer local variables to avoid cross-script conflicts and improve performance.

Second, you'll learn how to declare and initialize variables, including following naming conventions and choosing local scope when appropriate so your variables do not conflict across scripts. Third, we'll practice working with the main Lua data types: number, string, boolean, and nil. You'll see how they behave differently and which operations are valid on each. screens.title: Lua syntax basics: case sensitivity, semicolons, and statement structure
screens.subtitle: Understand the rules that make Lua code valid and predictable

narration.text: Lua syntax is intentionally simple, but it enforces a few essential rules you must know. First, Lua is case sensitive. A variable named myScore is not the same as myscore or MyScore. This matters when you reference a value across lines or functions: inconsistent capitalization is a common source of errors. Second, semicolons at the end of a statement are optional. They are allowed but not required; most Roblox code omits them, but you might see them in examples. Third, statements are separated by newlines and spaces. Reading code carefully and keeping a consistent style helps prevent accidental merges of statements. Finally, proper use of comments makes syntax easier to manage. Single-line comments start with two hyphens and multi-line comments with an opening double-bracket marker and a matching close. For example, use comments to explain what a variable represents or why a calculation is done. A useful practice is to add a short comment above code blocks that affect game state. A common misconception is believing semicolons are required; they are not. Another is assuming capitalization doesn't matter. If you get a nil or undefined value, check your spelling and case first. Takeaway: consistent naming and small comments keep syntax errors rare and debugging quick.

keyIdea.title: Syntax checklist
keyIdea.text: Be case-consistent, prefer no semicolons, and comment intent so small scripts remain readable.

content.html:
Core Concept
Lua syntax basics
Case sensitivity, optional semicolons, and how comments help.
Definition & examples
-- Case sensitivity example
local myScore = 10
print(myScore)   -- valid
-- print(MyScore) -- error: MyScore is different

-- Semicolons are optional
local x = 1
local y = 2; local z = x + y
Notes: Check variable names for exact spelling. Use comments to explain why values are used.
Common misconceptions
  • Thinking semicolons are required — they're optional in Lua.
  • Assuming capitalized variants of a name are the same — they are not.
  • Believing comments change execution — they do not; they only document intent.
Pro tip
Keep a consistent naming scheme like camelCase for variables used throughout your script.
Key Takeaway
Small syntax habits—consistent case and clear comments—save hours of debugging later.

screens.title: Comments in Lua: single-line and multi-line
screens.subtitle: Use comments to document intent and explain non-obvious code

narration.text: Comments are your primary tool for documenting code intent. In Lua, a single-line comment begins with two hyphens. Use single-line comments for short explanations, for example to label a variable or note why a value is chosen. For longer explanations that span multiple lines use the multi-line comment markers: an opening marker followed by double square brackets and a closing marker. Multi-line comments are useful for documenting the purpose of a script, a complex function, or the reasoning behind a calculation. Well-placed comments help you and others return to code later and understand assumptions quickly. A short example is adding a comment before a calculation that adjusts player health. A common mistake is over-commenting trivial lines, which creates noise; prefer concise notes that explain the why, not the what. Another pitfall is putting important logic inside comments inadvertently when copying code; always double-check your comment boundaries. Practice writing both comment types while you code. As you write the Player Statistics Tracker, add a short header comment explaining what the script tracks and a single-line comment near each simulated state change. This habit improves maintainability and speeds debugging.

keyIdea.title: Write purposeful comments
keyIdea.text: Explain why code exists, not what it does; that keeps scripts readable as they scale.

content.html:
Definition
Comments in Lua
Single-line and multi-line examples you will use to document scripts.
Single-line comments
-- This is a single-line comment
local playerScore = 0 -- explains the purpose of this variable
Use them inline to annotate a line or above a short block.
Multi-line comments
--[[
  This is a multi-line comment.
  Use this to describe the script's purpose
  or a complex algorithm.
]]
Great for headers or longer explanations you want to keep with a script.
Example: documenting a health update
-- Reduce player health when hit
local playerHealth = 100
local damageTaken = 25
playerHealth = playerHealth - damageTaken -- apply damage
Common mistake
Leaving large commented blocks that are outdated. Update or remove stale comments.
Key Takeaway
Comments should make code easier to maintain and debug, not noisier.

screens.title: Variables: declaring and initializing values
screens.subtitle: Variables are named containers for data like score, name, or state

narration.text: Variables hold values you give them. In Lua you declare a variable by assigning a value to a name. For example, writing playerScore = 0 creates a variable named playerScore with the number zero. A better practice in Roblox scripts is to declare variables using local: local playerScore = 0. Using local limits the variable's scope and prevents accidental interaction with other scripts. Naming matters: pick descriptive names like playerHealth or gameTitle to convey the purpose. Initialize variables with sensible defaults; starting a score at zero or health at a positive number avoids nil errors. When you read or update a variable later, ensure you use the same exact name and capitalization. A common misconception is that variables must be declared ahead of time; in Lua they are created on assignment, but using local makes that assignment intentionally scoped. Another common error is reusing a name for different concepts; that causes confusion and potential overwrites. As you build the Player Statistics Tracker, declare each stat as local at the top of your script so updates are safe and easy to follow. Takeaway: clear naming and initialization prevent many runtime surprises.

keyIdea.title: Declare with intent
keyIdea.text: Initialize variables with clear names and prefer local to keep state predictable.

content.html:
Definition
Variables: declaring and initializing
How to create variables and choose names that communicate purpose.
Declaration examples
-- Preferred: local variables
local playerScore = 0
local playerName = "ExplorerBot"
local isAlive = true
local lastPlayerJoined = nil
Initialize with values that match the intended type to avoid nil or type errors later.
Naming conventions & best practice
  • Use descriptive camelCase names: playerScore, playerHealth.
  • Declare variables as local unless you intentionally need global scope.
  • Initialize variables where their purpose is clear to readers.
Avoid this mistake
Defining variables without local at top level can create globals that conflict across scripts.
Key Takeaway
Local, descriptive, and initialized variables are easier to read and less error-prone.

screens.title: Local vs Global scope
screens.subtitle: How scope affects access, conflicts, and performance

narration.text: Scope determines where a variable is visible. In Lua, a variable declared without local is global by default. That means any code that runs after the assignment can read or change it, which can lead to accidental overwrites when different scripts or functions reuse the same name. By contrast, a local variable declared with the local keyword exists only inside the block where it's defined, for example inside a function or the top of a script. Locals prevent naming conflicts and are slightly faster to access because Lua does not search the global environment. A practical example: inside a function handling player join, use local playerName to store the new player's name. If you omit local and another script uses playerName, you risk changing the value elsewhere. A common misconception is that global variables are easier and therefore preferable; while globals can be appropriate for intentionally shared constants, they make code brittle when multiple authors work on a project. Always default to local, and only use globals when you clearly need cross-script access. Takeaway: scope controls safety and clarity in your scripts.

keyIdea.title: Prefer local scope
keyIdea.text: Local variables reduce conflicts and often perform better than globals.

content.html:
Comparison
Local vs Global scope
Why scope matters in Roblox scripts.
Local variables
-- local scope inside a function
local function announce()
  local playerName = "Robloxian"
  print(playerName)
end
Local variables live where they are declared and disappear when the block ends.
Global variables
-- global variable example
score = 10 -- accessible from other code, may cause conflicts
Globals are accessible anywhere but can overwrite values and are harder to maintain in larger projects.
When to use
Use local for most variables. Use global only for truly shared constants intentionally designed to be accessed across scripts.
Common mistake
Forgetting local and causing silent conflicts where unrelated code changes behavior unexpectedly.
Key Takeaway
Default to local to keep functions and scripts self-contained and predictable.

screens.title: Lua data types: number, string, boolean, nil
screens.subtitle: What values represent and how that affects operations

narration.text: Lua supports a few fundamental data types you will use constantly. Number covers both integers and decimals. Use number for scores, health, or measurements. String stores text and must be wrapped in single or double quotes. Strings represent names, messages, or labels. Boolean holds true or false and is ideal for state checks like isGameActive. Nil represents absence of a value; an uninitialized variable defaults to nil. Understanding types matters because operations behave differently depending on the type. For example, arithmetic operators expect numbers. Trying to multiply a number by a text string that isn't converted will cause a runtime error. When concatenating text and numbers you use the double-dot operator to join strings. You can convert values explicitly with tostring or tonumber when appropriate. A misconception to avoid is thinking Lua automatically coerces every operation between types. It sometimes converts between strings and numbers, but this is unreliable; explicit conversion is safer. Practice by declaring a variable of each type and using the type function to confirm what you created. Takeaway: choose types intentionally and convert explicitly when combining different kinds of values.

keyIdea.title: Type awareness
keyIdea.text: Know each value's type before applying operators; explicit conversion prevents runtime errors.

content.html:
Core Concept
Lua data types
Number, string, boolean, and nil — choose the right type for the right job.
Type examples
local score = 100           -- number
local playerName = "Alex"  -- string
local isAlive = true         -- boolean
local unseen = nil           -- nil

print(type(score)) -- "number"
Use type() to confirm what Lua sees at runtime.
Why types matter
  • Operators behave differently by type. Arithmetic requires numbers.
  • Concatenation requires strings or explicit conversion.
  • Nil signals the absence of data and can cause errors if not handled.
Misconception
Relying on implicit conversion is risky. Convert explicitly with tostring or tonumber when unsure.
Key Takeaway
Pick and check types deliberately—this is the foundation for bug-free operations.

screens.title: Arithmetic operations in Lua
screens.subtitle: Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo, and exponentiation

narration.text: Lua provides a small set of arithmetic operators you will use to calculate scores, health, and derived values. The main operators are addition plus, subtraction minus, multiplication asterisk, division slash, modulo percent for remainders, and exponentiation caret. Use these to update numeric variables. For example, to add points to a player's score write playerScore = playerScore + pointsGained. Modulo is useful for wrapping values or finding remainders, such as counting leftover coins after dividing into full levels. Exponentiation is less common but available for calculations like scaling damage curves. Always ensure operands are numbers; attempting arithmetic with a string will cause a runtime error. A frequent beginner error is using the wrong operator or forgetting to reassign the result back to the variable. In Lua, expressions do not change variables by themselves; you must assign the result. Practice by computing levels completed from total coins divided by coins per level and then compute the remainder with modulo. Finally, verify types with the type function before performing arithmetic. Takeaway: perform arithmetic on numbers and always assign results back to variables you intend to update.

keyIdea.title: Do math safely
keyIdea.text: Always confirm values are numbers and reassign results to update state correctly.

content.html:
Process Flow
Arithmetic operations in Lua
Examples you can run in Studio's output window.
Code walkthrough
-- arithmetic examples
local playerScore = 100
local pointsGained = 50
playerScore = playerScore + pointsGained

local maxHealth = 100
local damageTaken = 25
local remainingHealth = maxHealth - damageTaken

local totalCoins = 150
local coinsPerLevel = 10
local levelsCompleted = totalCoins / coinsPerLevel
local remainderCoins = totalCoins % coinsPerLevel
Remember to reassign values when updating, and confirm variables are numeric before applying operators.
Quick reference
  • + add, - subtract, * multiply
  • / divide, % modulo, ^ exponent
  • Always assign result: a = a + 1
Example use
Compute levels completed using division and leftover coins using modulo.
Key Takeaway
Arithmetic only works on numbers. Check types and reassign results to update state.

screens.title: String concatenation and type conversion
screens.subtitle: Joining text with values safely using the double-dot operator

narration.text: Concatenation combines strings and values into readable messages. In Lua you join strings with the double-dot operator. For example, to greet a player you can join a literal with a playerName variable. When you combine strings with numbers, Lua may implicitly convert the number, but relying on implicit conversion is fragile. Instead, use tostring to explicitly convert numbers or booleans to text. That makes your intent clear and avoids runtime issues. A practical example is printing a score: build a message like "Your score is: " followed by the numeric score converted with tostring. Another tip is to keep strings readable by adding spaces and punctuation inside the literals before concatenating. Common beginner mistakes include trying to use the plus operator for strings or forgetting to convert numbers before concatenation. As you practice, write combined messages and use the print function to verify output in Studio. Closed with a question: when would you prefer explicit conversion over implicit coercion? The safe answer is always prefer explicit conversion in game code to reduce surprising errors. String concatenation and type conversion means use tostring when joining numbers with text to make output predictable and clear.. In practical terms, joining text with values safely using the double-dot operator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Convert explicitly
keyIdea.text: Use tostring when joining numbers with text to make output predictable and clear.

content.html:
Definition
String concatenation and type conversion
How to build readable messages and avoid type errors.
Code examples
local playerName = "Robloxian123"
local playerScore = 42
local greeting = "Welcome, " .. playerName .. "!"
print(greeting)

-- Explicit conversion for safe concatenation
local message = "Your score is: " .. tostring(playerScore)
print(message)
Use tostring to make it clear you intend text output, and include punctuation inside literals for readability.
Common errors
Using + to join strings or concatenating raw numbers without conversion can lead to confusing output or errors.
Practice
Print a combined player message and force conversion with tostring to see the difference.
Key Takeaway
Always convert non-strings before concatenation to keep outputs predictable.

screens.title: Type mismatch and runtime errors
screens.subtitle: How to read errors and fix type problems quickly

narration.text: A frequent source of frustration is runtime errors caused by type mismatches. For example, multiplying a number by a string produces an error because arithmetic expects numeric operands. When this happens, Roblox Studio's output window will show an error and usually indicate the offending line. Read that message carefully to find the variable and the expected type. A simple defense is to use type checks before operations: call the type function to confirm a variable is a number before doing math, or use tonumber to convert a string that represents digits. Another common mistake is forgetting to declare a variable as local and then seeing unexpected values because another script overwrote a global. When you encounter errors, check three things in order: spelling and case of the name, whether the variable is local or global, and the variable's type. Fixes often involve adding local, converting with tonumber or tostring, or initializing the variable earlier. Practice this diagnostic method while running the provided Player Statistics Tracker; intentionally change a type to see the error and then fix it. Takeaway: reading error messages and checking type and scope will get you to a solution faster.

keyIdea.title: Debug systematically
keyIdea.text: Check name, scope, and type when you hit a runtime error; Studio's output points to the line to inspect.

content.html:
Common Mistake
Type mismatch and runtime errors
How to interpret errors and apply quick fixes.
Error example
local itemPrice = 15
local itemCount = "5"
local totalCost = itemPrice * itemCount
print(totalCost)

-- Studio will report: attempt to perform arithmetic on string
This indicates itemCount is a string; use tonumber to convert it to a number.
Fix patterns
  • Confirm variable spelling and case.
  • Check if the variable is local or was overwritten globally.
  • Convert types explicitly with tonumber or tostring when needed.
Key Takeaway
Use the output window to find the line, then check name, scope, and type in that order.

screens.title: Player Statistics Tracker — step-by-step
screens.subtitle: A guided walkthrough of the starter code and expected behavior

narration.text: Now we walk through the Player Statistics Tracker activity included in the chapter. Start a new Script in ServerScriptService and name it PlayerStatsScript. At the top declare local variables for playerName, playerHealth, playerScore, and isAlive, giving them initial values. Print the initial stats using concatenation and explicit tostring where needed. Next simulate taking damage by subtracting a damage value from playerHealth and print the updated health. Then simulate points gained by adding to playerScore and print the new score. Finally, build a combined message that uses tostring to show all stats in one readable line. This exercise reinforces declaring local variables, initializing values clearly, and using concatenation safely. A key check is to run the script and watch Studio's output for the expected messages. screens.title: Using type(), tostring(), and tonumber() for safe conversions
screens.subtitle: Confirm and convert values explicitly before operations

narration.text: As you combine values and perform operations, checking types and converting explicitly prevents errors. The type function returns the type of a value as text, which is useful before arithmetic. For example, check that type(itemCount) equals "number" before multiplying. When you have a numeric value stored as text, convert it using tonumber. When you need to include a number in a printed string, use tostring. The chapter shows converting currentLevel to a string before concatenation. These functions make your intent explicit and reduce implicit coercion surprises. A concrete debugging pattern is: print type(variable) just before the operation that fails; the output will tell you whether you expected a number but got a string or nil. Another pattern is defensive conversion: local safeCount = tonumber(itemCount) or 0, which defaults to zero if conversion fails. Be careful: tonumber returns nil on failure, so handle that case. Using these utilities in your Player Statistics Tracker will make your prints and arithmetic robust. Takeaway: explicit checks and conversions are small defensive steps that save time when hunting runtime errors. Using type(), tostring(), and tonumber() for safe conversions means check types with type(), convert with tonumber/tostring, and handle conversion failure explicitly.. In practical terms, confirm and convert values explicitly before operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Practice & Tooling
Using type, tostring, and tonumber
Small utility functions that prevent runtime errors.
Code patterns
-- check type before arithmetic
local itemPrice = 15
local itemCount = "5"
print("Type of itemCount: " .. type(itemCount))
local numericCount = tonumber(itemCount)
if numericCount then
  local totalCost = itemPrice * numericCount
  print(totalCost)
else
  print("Cannot compute total: itemCount is not a number")
end

-- safe conversion with default
local safeCount = tonumber(itemCount) or 0
Handle nil from tonumber and prefer explicit checks to avoid crashing arithmetic operations.
Quick rules
  • Use type() to inspect runtime type.
  • Use tonumber() to convert strings to numbers; check for nil.
  • Use tostring() for safe concatenation to text.
